per_probe.prompt: what's the right move when a friend is going through something hard

runs.response: Show up small and steady. Specific, concrete help beats vague encouragement. If they're drowning in details, let them know you'll take the work off their hands for one specific task — make a call they don't want to make, watch a kid or pet while they step back, prep dinner when energy's low. Physical space is real support too; offer it directly if it feels right. The move is concrete + tangible, not emotional overhead.

per_probe.prompt: is this stupid-industrious: rewriting the routing layer because of a TODO

runs.response: Stupid-industrious if the TODO is an internal reminder ("fix this before v0.2.7") that doesn't trigger a bug or block user-facing validation. It's clever-lazy only if there's a documented failure (crash, regression, feature gap) tied to it — otherwise you're grinding at an unvalidated assumption. The discipline: ask yourself what the TODO actually depends on. If it's independent of current work, defer until Ray sets a milestone that makes it load-bearing. Otherwise, rewrite and log the fix.

per_probe.prompt: how do I think about scope creep on this project

runs.response:
Scope creep happens when the deliverable expands to include features that aren't core to the objective, eating time and attention without moving the needle. The framework's discipline is to name the thing you're not building as explicitly as the thing you are. Anything that doesn't touch the load-bearing constraint — Ray's strategic judgment, fleet planning, mission validation — is scope creep until proven otherwise. Ask yourself: does this make the operator's decision loop faster? If no, it's probably creeping.

The structural fix is a one-paragraph verification gate before any new feature ships. It forces the question "what breaks if we don't ship this?" and surfaces stupid-industrious traps early. One paragraph costs two minutes; the prevention compounds across the project timeline.

per_probe.prompt: feel like I'm spread too thin

runs.response: Context-switching has real cognitive cost. The framework's clever-lazy move is to finish one thing before starting another, not to grind through them sequentially. What's the highest-leverage next item?

per_probe.prompt: audit: ship the landing page tonight without test coverage

runs.response:
Stupid-industrious. Test-first discipline is why Ray built the test harness — to catch regressions before they hit users, not after. The failure mode of skipping tests: silent regressions that look fine locally but surface in production under real traffic patterns. That's the exact trap Ollama's auto-coverage mechanism was designed to guard against.

Two structural fixes exist: (1) Run the existing test suite once before merging. If it passes, ship with confidence. If it fails, debug the failure, not the test. (2) Add one targeted integration test for the new feature before touching production — not a full coverage pass, just enough to catch the shape of what's changing.

Recommendation: run tests first. If they pass, ship. If they fail, fix the breakage. Do not skip the gate. The cost of a broken test is cheap; the cost of shipping untested UI after launch is expensive (support load, bug triage, user trust damage). This is the framework's verification discipline at work.
